julius-caesar.name: Julius Caesar
julius-caesar.summary: Roman general and statesman, 100 to 44 BC, who became dictator of the Republic, expanded Roman territory through the Gallic Wars, and was assassinated in 44 BC.

strabo.name: Strabo
strabo.summary: Greek geographer (64/63 BC to about 24 AD) best known for his Geographica, a descriptive survey of the peoples and places known in his time.

colchester.name: Colchester
colchester.summary: A city in north-eastern Essex, England, built on the site of Camulodunum, the first major city and capital of Roman Britain, giving it a claim to be Britain's first city.

celtic-art.name: Celtic art
celtic-art.summary: A term for the art of Celtic-speaking peoples across Iron Age Europe, especially from the La Tène period (5th to 1st centuries BC), noted for geometric decoration over figurative imagery.

gallo-roman-culture.name: Gallo-Roman culture
gallo-roman-culture.summary: The blending of Gaulish and Roman culture, language, and customs in Roman Gaul, which persisted in parts of southern and central Gaul into the 7th century despite barbarian invasions.

maiden-castle-dorset.name: Maiden Castle
maiden-castle-dorset.summary: Iron Age hillfort near Dorchester, England, expanded around 450 BCE into the largest hillfort in Britain and occupied into the Roman period.

cadbury-castle-somerset.name: Cadbury Castle
cadbury-castle-somerset.summary: A Bronze and Iron Age hillfort in Somerset, England, long associated with the legend of King Arthur's Camelot.

hillfort.name: Hillforts
hillfort.summary: Fortified settlements built on high ground for defense, common across Bronze and Iron Age Europe and sometimes home to as many as 1,000 people.

hallstatt-culture.name: Hallstatt culture
hallstatt-culture.summary: A Western and Central European archaeological culture spanning the Late Bronze Age through Early Iron Age (12th-6th centuries BC), commonly linked to Proto-Celtic peoples.

merovingian-dynasty.name: Merovingian dynasty
merovingian-dynasty.summary: The ruling family of the Franks from the mid-5th century until 751, who united the Franks and conquered much of Gaul; known for wearing their hair long as a mark of royal legitimacy.

merovingian-art-and-architecture.name: Merovingian art
merovingian-art-and-architecture.summary: The art of the Frankish Merovingian dynasty, spanning the 5th to 8th centuries in present-day France, Benelux and part of Germany, blending 'barbarian' animal-style decoration with Late Antique influences.

clovis-i.name: Clovis I
clovis-i.summary: First king to unite the Franks under one ruler (c. 466–511), founder of the Merovingian dynasty and a foundational figure in the history of France.

alesia-city.name: Alesia
alesia-city.summary: Capital of the Gallic Mandubii tribe, a Celtic hillfort captured by Julius Caesar during the Gallic Wars and later a Gallo-Roman town, thought to have stood at Mont-Auxois in Burgundy, France.

vercingetorix.name: Vercingetorix
vercingetorix.summary: A Gallic chieftain of the Arverni (c. 82–46 BC) who united the Gauls against Rome, won at Gergovia, then surrendered at Alesia in 52 BC and was later executed.

boudica.name: Boudica
boudica.summary: Queen of the British Iceni tribe who led a failed uprising against Roman rule in Britain in AD 60 or 61, later remembered as a national heroine.

iceni.name: Iceni
iceni.summary: An ancient British tribe of the Iron Age and early Roman era based in what is now Norfolk, whose queen Boudica led a major revolt against Roman rule in AD 60–61.

camulodunum.name: Camulodunum
camulodunum.summary: The Roman name for what is now Colchester, England, and the first capital of Roman Britain; it began as a Celtic stronghold before becoming a major Roman colony.

londinium.name: Londinium
londinium.summary: The Roman name for London, founded around 47–50 AD, which grew to become the largest city in Roman Britain.

gaius-suetonius-paulinus.name: Suetonius Paulinus
gaius-suetonius-paulinus.summary: Roman general active AD 40–69, best known as the commander who defeated Boudica's revolt in Britain.

hadrian-s-wall.name: Hadrian's Wall
hadrian-s-wall.summary: A Roman defensive wall across northern England, begun in AD 122 under Emperor Hadrian, running 73 miles from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

hadrian.name: Hadrian
hadrian.summary: Roman emperor from 117 to 138, born in Hispania, who abandoned Trajan's territorial expansion in favor of stable borders and personally visited almost every province of the empire.

wallsend.name: Wallsend
wallsend.summary: An English town in Tyne and Wear marking the eastern end of Hadrian's Wall.

bowness-on-solway.name: Bowness-on-Solway
bowness-on-solway.summary: A village in Cumbria, England, on the Solway Firth, marking the western end of Hadrian's Wall.

claudius.name: Claudius
claudius.summary: Roman emperor from AD 41 to 54, the first born outside Italy, who proved an able administrator despite being excluded from public life earlier due to illness.

classis-britannica.name: Classis Britannica
classis-britannica.summary: Roman provincial naval fleet that controlled the English Channel and waters around Britannia, mainly moving troops and supplies rather than fighting battles.

aulus-plautius.name: Aulus Plautius
aulus-plautius.summary: Roman general and politician of the 1st century who began the Roman conquest of Britain in 43 CE and served as its first governor until 46.

fosse-way.name: Fosse Way
fosse-way.summary: A Roman road built in Britain in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, linking Exeter in the southwest to Lincoln in the northeast.

arverni.name: Arverni
arverni.summary: A powerful Gallic tribe of the late Iron Age based in what is now Auvergne, France, that rivaled the Aedui and later led resistance to Rome.

battle-of-gergovia.name: Battle of Gergovia
battle-of-gergovia.summary: A 52 BC battle in Gaul where Vercingetorix's Gallic forces defeated Julius Caesar's besieging Roman army after miscommunication let Gallic cavalry rout the confused Romans.

tacitus.name: Tacitus
tacitus.summary: A Roman historian and politician (c. 56–120 AD) whose works Annals and Histories chronicled the empire, regarded as one of Rome's greatest historians.

caledonians.name: Caledonians
caledonians.summary: A Celtic tribal confederacy in Iron Age and Roman-era Scotland who fought the Roman Empire; Rome never fully conquered their territory, known as Caledonia.

battle-of-mons-graupius.name: Battle of Mons Graupius
battle-of-mons-graupius.summary: A Roman military victory in what is now Scotland, likely fought in AD 83 or 84, described by the historian Tacitus though details of his account are debated.

calgacus.name: Calgacus
calgacus.summary: A chieftain of the Caledonian Confederacy described by the Roman historian Tacitus as leading resistance against Rome; some historians debate whether he actually existed.

anglesey.name: Anglesey
anglesey.summary: An island off the northwest coast of Wales, the largest island in Wales, and a heartland of the Welsh language.

boudican-revolt.name: Boudican revolt
boudican-revolt.summary: An uprising by Celtic Britons against Roman rule around AD 60–61, led by Queen Boudica after Rome broke an agreement over her husband's succession, ending in a decisive Roman victory.

gnaeus-julius-agricola.name: Agricola
gnaeus-julius-agricola.summary: Roman general and politician (40-93 CE) who, as governor of Britain from 77, completed the conquest of Wales and northern England and led forces into Scotland.

battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains.name: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains.summary: A 451 CE battle in Gaul where a Roman-Visigothic coalition under Flavius Aetius and Theodoric I fought off Attila's Huns, one of the last major campaigns of the Western Roman Empire.

flavius-aetius.name: Flavius Aetius
flavius-aetius.summary: A Roman general and the most powerful man in the Western Roman Empire from 433 to 454, who defeated Attila the Hun at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451 before being assassinated by Emperor Valentinian III.

theodoric-i.name: Theodoric I
theodoric-i.summary: King of the Visigoths from 418 to 451, famed for helping stop Attila the Hun at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451, where he was killed.

attila.name: Attila
attila.summary: Ruler of the Huns from 434 until his death in 453, known as "the Scourge of God," who invaded the Balkans, Gaul and Italy but never took Rome or Constantinople.

foederati.name: Foederati
foederati.summary: Peoples, cities or barbarian groups bound to Rome by treaty, who received benefits in exchange for military help and, especially under the empire, were often allowed to settle within its borders.

quintus-petillius-cerialis.name: Quintus Petillius Cerialis
quintus-petillius-cerialis.summary: A Roman general and administrator (c. AD 30 – after AD 83) who served in Britain during Boudica's rebellion, later crushed Julius Civilis's revolt, and returned to Britain as its governor.

cassius-dio.name: Cassius Dio
cassius-dio.summary: Roman historian and senator of Greek origin (c. 165–c. 235) who wrote an 80-volume history of Rome spanning roughly 1,000 years.

andraste.name: Andraste
andraste.summary: An Icenic war goddess invoked by the British queen Boudica during her revolt against Roman rule in AD 60, whose name has been translated as "unconquerable".

caligula.name: Caligula
caligula.summary: Third Roman emperor, reigning AD 37 to 41 after succeeding Tiberius; ancient sources describe his early rule as fair before he grew increasingly cruel and extravagant.

suetonius.name: Suetonius
suetonius.summary: Roman historian (c. AD 69 – after AD 122) best known for The Twelve Caesars, a set of biographies of twelve successive Roman rulers from Julius Caesar to Domitian.

commentarii-de-bello-gallico.name: Commentarii de Bello Gallico
commentarii-de-bello-gallico.summary: Julius Caesar's first-hand, third-person account of his nine years fighting Celtic and Germanic peoples in Gaul, long used as a mainstay of Latin instruction for its simple, direct prose.

vindolanda-tablets.name: Vindolanda tablets
vindolanda-tablets.summary: Wooden leaf-tablets with ink writing from the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, found at the Roman fort of Vindolanda in northern England; among the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain.

ogham.name: Ogham
ogham.summary: An early medieval alphabet used to write early Irish, with roughly 400 surviving inscriptions on stone monuments in Ireland and western Britain.

ausonius.name: Ausonius
ausonius.summary: Roman poet and teacher of rhetoric from Burdigala (c. 310–395) who tutored the future Emperor Gratian, later made consul; best known for the poems Mosella and Ephemeris.

bordeaux.name: Bordeaux
bordeaux.summary: A city on the river Garonne in southwestern France, now known as a world capital of wine with many vineyards and the world's main wine fair.

gratian.name: Gratian
gratian.summary: Emperor of the Western Roman Empire from 367 to 383, eldest son of Valentinian I, who favored Catholicism and was eventually murdered after being abandoned by his army.

claudia-severa.name: Claudia Severa
claudia-severa.summary: A literate Roman woman, wife of fort commander Aelius Brocchus, who around 100 AD sent a birthday invitation to Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of commander Flavius Cerialis — probably the best-known item among the Vindolanda Tablets.

sulpicia-lepidina.name: Sulpicia Lepidina
sulpicia-lepidina.summary: Wife of a Roman army prefect stationed at Vindolanda in Roman Britain in the early 2nd century AD, known from surviving personal correspondence.

bloomberg-tablets.name: Bloomberg tablets
bloomberg-tablets.summary: A collection of 405 wooden tablets found at London's Bloomberg building site, dating from 50 to 80 CE, the earliest written documents ever found in Britain.

sidonius-apollinaris.name: Sidonius Apollinaris
sidonius-apollinaris.summary: A Gallo-Roman poet, diplomat and bishop of Clermont (c. 430–481/490) who led the city's defense against the Visigoths and is called the most important surviving author from 5th-century Gaul.

trajan-s-forum.name: Trajan's Forum
trajan-s-forum.summary: The last of the Imperial fora built in ancient Rome, designed by the architect Apollodorus of Damascus.

claudian.name: Claudian
claudian.summary: Latin poet (c. 370–404 AD) at the court of Emperor Honorius in Milan, closely tied to the general Stilicho, writing poems in hexameters and elegiac couplets.

theodosius-i.name: Theodosius I
theodosius-i.summary: Roman emperor from 379 to 395, also called Theodosius the Great, who established Nicene Christianity as orthodox doctrine and was the last emperor to rule the whole Roman Empire.

honorius.name: Honorius
honorius.summary: Roman emperor from 393 to 423 who, under regent Stilicho, ruled the Western Roman Empire during the sack of Rome in 410.

picts.name: Picts
picts.summary: A group of peoples living in what is now Scotland north of the Firth of Forth during the Early Middle Ages, whose name may derive from the Latin word for 'painted'.

annals-tacitus.name: Annals of Tacitus
annals-tacitus.summary: A history of the Roman Empire by the senator Tacitus, covering the reigns of Tiberius to Nero (AD 14–68) and considered his masterpiece.

praetorian-prefecture-of-gaul.name: Praetorian Prefecture of Gaul
praetorian-prefecture-of-gaul.summary: One of four large administrative divisions of the late Roman Empire in the 4th century, covering its Gaulish territories.

alemanni.name: Alemanni
alemanni.summary: A confederation of Germanic peoples that emerged east of the Upper Rhine in the 3rd century AD, later seizing Roman land and giving rise to the region called Alamannia.

bissula.name: Bissula
bissula.summary: An Alemannic woman captured by the Romans in 368 who became a slave, then freed lover, of the Roman poet Ausonius, who wrote a poem about her.

elder-futhark.name: Elder Futhark
elder-futhark.summary: The oldest form of the runic alphabets, used by Germanic peoples from the 2nd to 8th centuries; its reading was forgotten until deciphered in 1865.

riothamus.name: Riothamus
riothamus.summary: A Romano-British military leader active around AD 470 who fought the Goths alongside the declining Western Roman Empire, sometimes suggested as an inspiration for the legendary King Arthur.

king-arthur.name: King Arthur
king-arthur.summary: A legendary king of Britain and central figure of medieval literature, first portrayed in early Welsh sources fighting the Anglo-Saxons; most historians doubt he was a real person.

servius-the-grammarian.name: Servius the Grammarian
servius-the-grammarian.summary: Roman grammarian of the late 4th and early 5th centuries, regarded as the most learned man of his generation in Italy, best known for his commentaries on Virgil.

virgil.name: Virgil
virgil.summary: Ancient Roman poet (70–19 BC) of the Augustan age who wrote the Eclogues, the Georgics and the epic Aeneid, becoming a hugely influential model for later Western literature.

pytheas.name: Pytheas
pytheas.summary: Greek geographer and explorer from Massalia (born c. 350 BC) who sailed to Northern Europe around 325 BC, circumnavigating Britain and becoming the first to describe the Arctic and the midnight sun.

massalia.name: Massalia
massalia.summary: An ancient Greek colony founded around 600 BCE on the Mediterranean coast, a major trading center whose ruins underlie modern Marseille, France's oldest city.

coligny-calendar.name: Coligny calendar
coligny-calendar.summary: A bronze plaque inscribed with a 5-year lunisolar calendar, made in Roman Gaul in the 2nd century CE and the key evidence for reconstructing an ancient Celtic calendar.

coligny-ain.name: Coligny, Ain
coligny-ain.summary: A small commune in the Ain department of eastern France, where the Coligny calendar was unearthed in 1897.

lugdunum-museum.name: Lugdunum (museum)
lugdunum-museum.summary: Museum of Gallo-Roman civilisation in Lyon, opened in 1975 near the city's Roman theatre, displaying Roman and Celtic artifacts; renamed Lugdunum in 2017.

insular-celts.name: Insular Celts
insular-celts.summary: Celtic-speaking peoples of the British Isles and Brittany, including the Britons, Picts and Gaels, who followed an ancient Celtic religion overseen by druids.

samhain.name: Samhain
samhain.summary: A Gaelic festival on 1 November marking the end of harvest and start of winter, with roots in Celtic pagan tradition and links to Irish mythology.

beltane.name: Beltane
beltane.summary: The Gaelic May Day festival marking the start of summer, historically observed in Ireland, Scotland and the Isle of Man with protective bonfires and rituals.

aquae-sulis.name: Aquae Sulis
aquae-sulis.summary: Roman-era name for what is now Bath, England, built around natural hot springs; it grew into a major temple and bath complex by the 3rd century AD.

diodorus-siculus.name: Diodorus Siculus
diodorus-siculus.summary: Ancient Greek historian from Sicily (1st century BC) who wrote the 40-book universal history Bibliotheca historica, covering world history up to about 60 BC.

pliny-the-elder.name: Pliny the Elder
pliny-the-elder.summary: A Roman author, naturalist and military commander (23/24–79 AD) who wrote the 37-volume encyclopedia Natural History and died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius.

natural-history-pliny.name: Natural History
natural-history-pliny.summary: Encyclopedic Latin work by Pliny the Elder, published around AD 77, the largest surviving single work from the Roman Empire, covering topics from astronomy to art and precious stones.

gaulish.name: Gaulish
gaulish.summary: An extinct Celtic language spoken in parts of continental Europe before and during Roman times, attested in around 800 surviving inscriptions.

thule.name: Thule
thule.summary: A legendary, extremely remote northern land described by ancient Greek and Roman writers, later variously identified with places like Iceland, Greenland or Scandinavia.

dicaearchus.name: Dicaearchus
dicaearchus.summary: A Greek philosopher and geographer, a student of Aristotle, who wrote on geography, the history of Greece, ancient poets, philosophy, and politics.

timaeus-historian.name: Timaeus of Tauromenium
timaeus-historian.summary: Ancient Greek historian (c. 356/350–260 BC) regarded as the leading authority on the history of the Greek West for centuries.

battle-of-alesia.name: Battle of Alesia
battle-of-alesia.summary: The climactic siege of September 52 BC in which Julius Caesar's Roman army defeated Vercingetorix's confederation of Gallic tribes, ending Gallic independence and ranking among Caesar's greatest military achievements.

britannia.name: Britannia
britannia.summary: National personification of Great Britain as a helmeted female warrior, originally a Latin name the Romans used for Britain and, after 43 AD, for their province there.

prasutagus.name: Prasutagus
prasutagus.summary: King of the Iceni, a Celtic tribe in what is now Norfolk, and husband of Boudica; his death around AD 60-61 and the Romans' seizure of his kingdom helped trigger her revolt.

carausius.name: Carausius
carausius.summary: A Roman military commander from Belgic Gaul who seized power in Britain and northern Gaul in 286, ruling seven years as self-declared 'Emperor of the North' before his assassination.

menapii.name: Menapii
menapii.summary: A Belgic tribe that lived near the North Sea around present-day Cassel during the Iron Age and Roman period.

allectus.name: Allectus
allectus.summary: A Roman-Britannic usurper who ruled Britain and northern Gaul from 293 to 296 AD, dying around 296.

trajan.name: Trajan
trajan.summary: Roman emperor from 98 to 117 CE, one of the Five Good Emperors, whose conquests brought the empire to its greatest territorial extent; born in what is now southern Spain.

celtillus.name: Celtillus
celtillus.summary: A Gallic nobleman of the Arverni people and father of Vercingetorix, said to be the 'foremost man of all Gaul,' who was killed by his own people for trying to seize kingship.

aedui.name: Aedui
aedui.summary: Gallic people who lived between the Loire and Saône rivers, among Rome's earliest allies in Gaul and later admitted to the Roman Senate.

marcus-vipsanius-agrippa.name: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa
marcus-vipsanius-agrippa.summary: Roman general and statesman (c.63-12 BC), a close ally of Augustus known for his naval victory at Actium and for building the original Pantheon.

lugdunum.name: Lugdunum
lugdunum.summary: Roman city founded in 43 BC on the site of modern Lyon, France, serving as capital of Gallia Lugdunensis with a population possibly reaching 200,000; birthplace of emperors Claudius and Caracalla.

gergovia.name: Gergovia
gergovia.summary: A Gaulish hilltop town in Auvergne, capital of the Arverni, where Vercingetorix's forces defeated Julius Caesar's army in 52 BC.

cunobelinus.name: Cunobelinus
cunobelinus.summary: King in pre-Roman Britain from about AD 9 to AD 40, called 'King of the Britons' by the Roman historian Suetonius; controlled much of southeastern Britain and may have been a client king of Rome.

catuvellauni.name: Catuvellauni
catuvellauni.summary: A Celtic tribe or state of southeastern Britain before the Roman conquest, centred on modern St Albans, believed to have led resistance to Rome's invasion in AD 43.

trinovantes.name: Trinovantes
trinovantes.summary: A Celtic tribe of pre-Roman Britain based north of the Thames estuary, bordered by the Iceni and Catuvellauni, with their capital at Camulodunum, modern Colchester.

atrebates.name: Atrebates
atrebates.summary: Belgic tribe originally from the Artois region of Gaul that fought Caesar, later settled in Britain under kings including Commius and Verica, before falling under Roman rule.

verica.name: Verica
verica.summary: A British client king of Rome in the early 1st century AD, ruling the Atrebates from around Chichester until his kingdom was conquered and he was expelled around 42 AD.

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.summary: Founder of the Roman Empire, ruling as its first emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14, and known earlier as Octavian.

tetrarchy.name: Tetrarchy
tetrarchy.summary: The system devised by Emperor Diocletian to rule the Roman Empire through two senior emperors and two junior successors, in place from 293 to 324 CE.

ancient-celtic-religion.name: Celtic paganism
ancient-celtic-religion.summary: The polytheistic religion of the ancient Celtic peoples of Europe, worshipping gods such as Lugus and Taranis, with druids as priests and ceremonies held in sacred groves.

joseph-of-arimathea.name: Joseph of Arimathea
joseph-of-arimathea.summary: Biblical figure who took responsibility for burying Jesus after his crucifixion, described in the Gospels as a member of the Sanhedrin or a rich disciple; many later medieval legends grew around him.

glastonbury.name: Glastonbury
glastonbury.summary: A town in Somerset, England, inhabited since Neolithic times and long dominated by Glastonbury Abbey, one of medieval England's most important abbeys.

lucius-of-britain.name: Lucius of Britain
lucius-of-britain.summary: Legendary 2nd-century king of the Britons credited with introducing Christianity to Britain by asking Pope Eleutherius to be made a Christian.

gennadius-of-massilia.name: Gennadius of Massilia
gennadius-of-massilia.summary: A 5th-century Christian priest, monk and historian who died around 496, best known for a biographical work continuing one by Jerome.

augustine-of-hippo.name: Augustine of Hippo
augustine-of-hippo.summary: Christian theologian and Bishop of Hippo (354–430), one of history's most influential philosophers, known for works like Confessions and The City of God.

gaels.name: Gaels
gaels.summary: Insular Celtic peoples native to Ireland, Scotland and the Isle of Man, associated with the Gaelic languages and kingdoms such as Dál Riata and Alba.

la-t-ne-culture.name: La Tène culture
la-t-ne-culture.summary: A European Iron Age culture that flourished from about 450 BC until the Roman conquest, spanning France, Central Europe and beyond, known for its swirling decorative metalwork style.

etruscan-civilization.name: Etruscans
etruscan-civilization.summary: A civilization of ancient Italy formed by a federation of city-states, with the earliest identifiably Etruscan culture dating from about 900 BC and its territory reaching its greatest extent around 500 BC.

golasecca-culture.name: Golasecca culture
golasecca-culture.summary: Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age culture (9th–4th centuries BC) in northern Italy, named for its type-site near Golasecca and spread across a wide area south of the Alps.

posidonius.name: Posidonius
posidonius.summary: A Greek Stoic philosopher, astronomer and polymath (c. 135–51 BC) from Apamea, Syria, whose lost writings on science and geography influenced later scholars.

gallic-wars.name: Gallic Wars
gallic-wars.summary: Rome's 58–50 BC campaigns under Julius Caesar against the Gauls, Britons, and Germanic tribes, ending with the decisive Battle of Alesia and Roman conquest of all of Gaul.

pausanias-geographer.name: Pausanias (geographer)
pausanias-geographer.summary: A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer, c. 110 to 180, whose Description of Greece is a key source linking classical literature to archaeological sites.
